subtopics.name: Investigating the Need for Chlorophyll, Light & Carbon Dioxide

parts.problem_md:
When an aquatic plant is exposed to light, it produces bubbles of oxygen gas.

Plan an investigation to determine the relationship between light intensity and the volume of oxygen gas produced by the aquatic plant.

You are provided with the apparatus shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Diagram of an aquatic plant under an inverted funnel in water, with a test tube above collecting gas bubbles produced by photosynthesis](assets/001-diagram-of-an-aquatic-plant-under-an-inverted-fu.png)

**Fig.2.1**

You may use any other common laboratory apparatus in your plan.

In your plan, include:

- any **additional** apparatus and chemicals that you will use
- a brief description of the method, explaining any safety precautions you will take
- what you will measure
- which variables you will control
- how you will process your results to form a conclusion.

You may include a labelled diagram.

You may include a results table (you are not required to enter any readings in the table).
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One mark from each section, plus any other two marks:
> 
> **Apparatus / chemicals**
> 
> - Lamp / suitable named light source **[1 mark]**
> - Gas syringe / measuring cylinder **[1 mark]**
> - Named timing device / named apparatus for varying light intensity / ruler **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Method and safety precautions**
> 
> - Method described clearly enough that another student could obtain suitable results **[1 mark]**
> - Safety precaution specific to water and electricity / hot lamps **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Measurements**
> 
> - Suitable way of varying and recording light intensity, e.g. distance of lamp from plant, brightness, number of lamps **[1 mark]**
> - Suitable way of recording volume of gas, e.g. displacement of water in a measuring cylinder **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Control variables**
> 
> - Concentration of CO<sub>2</sub>; temperature of water; another valid variable e.g. wavelength of light **[1 mark]**
> 
> **Processing results and conclusion**
> 
> - Comparing volume per unit time for each intensity **[1 mark]**
> - Using repeated measurements at each intensity to identify/exclude anomalies **[1 mark]**
> - Plotting a graph of volume of gas against light intensity **[1 mark]**
> 
> Apparatus must be relevant to the method described; marks may be awarded from a labelled diagram/results table/suggested graph axes; safety precaution must link to a specific hazard relevant to the method; control variables must be appropriate to the method

> **[exam-tip]**
> For any practical-planning question, structure your answer under the same five headings examiners mark against — apparatus, method/safety, measurements, control variables, and processing/conclusion — so you don't miss a whole category of marks.

parts.problem_md:
Plants photosynthesise.

State the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - 6CO<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> + 6O<sub>2</sub> **[2 marks]**
> 
> Accept reactants in any order; accept products in any order; ignore anything written over the arrow

> **[exam-tip]**
> Learn the balanced symbol equation exactly, including all six coefficients — a common mistake is remembering the word equation but forgetting to balance the symbol version.

parts.problem_md:
A student investigates photosynthesis using the set-up shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Diagram of two potted plants in clear plastic bags: plant X with a substance releasing carbon dioxide, plant Y with a substance absorbing carbon dioxide.](assets/002-diagram-of-two-potted-plants-in-clear-plastic-ba.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

The student puts the plants in the same warm room with plenty of light.

After three days, the student uses iodine solution to test a leaf from each plant.

Fig. 2.2 shows the results.

![Diagram comparing two leaves: plant X leaf shaded blue-black and plant Y leaf shaded yellow-brown, illustrating different leaf colouration.](assets/003-diagram-comparing-two-leaves-plant-x-leaf-shaded.png)

**Fig. 2.2**

(i) Complete the sentences to explain the results in Fig. 2.2.

The colour of the iodine solution shows that only the leaf from plant X contains .................................................. .

This investigation shows that photosynthesis requires the presence of .................................................. .

[2]

(ii) State the name of the green pigment needed for photosynthesis.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) Starch **[1 mark]**
> - (i) Carbon dioxide **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Chlorophyll **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A blue-black result with iodine confirms starch is present, which in turn confirms photosynthesis has occurred — so a blank iodine test (yellow-brown) tells you a factor needed for photosynthesis (here, CO2) was missing.

parts.problem_md:
Photosynthesis is an enzyme-controlled reaction.

Fig. 2.3 shows the effect of temperature on the rate of photosynthesis for three different plants.

![Graph showing rate of photosynthesis versus temperature for plants Q, R and S, with each curve rising to an optimum then falling, R peaking at highest temperature](assets/004-graph-showing-rate-of-photosynthesis-versus-temp.png)

(i) Identify the temperature at which the rate of photosynthesis for plant **Q** is highest.

[1]

(ii) In a desert, temperatures are often higher than 40 °C.

Explain why plant S would not survive in a desert.

Use the word enzyme in your answer.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> - (i) 30 °C **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Enzymes work best at lower temperatures / the enzyme stops working above 25 °C **[1 mark]**
> - (ii) Photosynthesis stops, so no glucose/sugar/carbohydrates are produced **[1 mark]**
> 
> Accept a value in the range 28–30 °C; accept enzymes are not active at 40 °C

> **[exam-tip]**
> Above its optimum temperature, an enzyme denatures and stops working entirely — don't confuse this with simply "working more slowly", which only applies below the optimum.

parts.problem_md:
An aquatic plant is placed in a beaker of water containing hydrogencarbonate indicator and kept in the dark.

Which colour will the hydrogencarbonate indicator be after 24 hours?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- In the dark, the plant cannot photosynthesise, so it only respires and releases carbon dioxide
- Carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, making the solution more acidic and turning the hydrogencarbonate indicator yellow
